As the administration has shifted its focus and strategy from gun control to mass incarceration, the federal government's efforts to fight violent crime have been slowed by concerns raised over an executive order that critics say would have allowed illegal gun transfers to be stopped and convicted without a trial or evidence.
Now that the president has set foot in New York, a major legislative showdown over the proposal to overhaul the nation's gun laws might have its biggest political payoff yet, according to some senior administration officials who reviewed the administration's actions in Washington on Monday.
President Obama said Monday that he wants Congress to hold to his promise to use "the power of his office"—that is, by invoking his own executive authority—to help reduce gun violence.
"I believe it has become imperative that we build on President Obama's recent actions to implement a major expansion of background checks to gun purchases, in order to keep guns out of the hands of young, vulnerable, low-income, law abiding individuals," Mr. Obama said.
Officials said that Mr. Obama made his decision as an executive, which requires the president to sign on to the policy before he can act.
"We have made clear to the president that he is confident that we will continue to have great success moving forward," a senior Obama official said.
Some administration officials were skeptical, saying that it could take months or even years for Obama to sign the order.
"It was a decision made at the beginning of his tenure, which we don't know is going to be permanent," said former Justice Department lawyer Paul Burt, who chaired the Obama Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel from 2007 to 2012 as deputy legal adviser. He said that the government's legal teams could find the president willing to act with a different set of rules, including the so-called "preemption" of executive orders, which would allow the government to take actions to prevent gun violence but make it easier for gun owners to obtain access to guns. Mr. Burt said that in the absence of that type of order, Mr. Obama is unlikely to be able to have this kind of impact if a person is able to obtain a gun.
"We think it is quite a significant development to put a stop to this, given the way the law was going," he said.

It did provide for the Department of Justice to create a "kill list'' of any U.S. person involved in terrorist plots, and it provided for the Department of Justice to impose specific limitations on the amount of the government's collection of information on the person in question.
The law also prohibited "the United States from conducting business with, or attempting to have in connection with any person suspected of carrying out any offense in the United States on U.S. soil" but does not ban activities by members of Congress that may violate the law and not allow the government to collect any information. What is known as "defense of persons who have served on or participated in the terrorist attacks" applies to U.S. citizens who served in terrorist acts abroad but have not been implicated in those acts or are in "preventive action."
